## All the sounds side by side

Play down the column and listen. The violin, clarinet and harmonica hold a steady note, every stem on a line. The kalimba's stems are off the lines, but its click fades almost at once and leaves a clean note. The piano's sit a little sharp of the lines. The drum's are off the lines and die fast: a thud.

Gray lines are whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency; stem height is how strongly each frequency starts. For the bowed and blown three, the stems are the frequencies in the sound, which the steady bow or breath keeps exactly on the lines ([page 6b](harmonica.qmd) explains why a steady repetition does this).




## How to read this series

The idea behind every page is laid out on [The spectrum of an operator](spectrum.qmd). Every page opens with a puzzle you can hear or see and a short summary of how the recipe answers it. Then each instrument page derives the instrument's operator from Newton's law, step by step, and works out its spectrum, the frequencies (page 0 comes before any operator; pages 9 and 10 reuse the operators of pages 8 and 6). Only proofs and side calculations are folded away; each fold says what mathematics it needs beyond high school, if any. Technical words and symbols link to the [glossary](glossary.qmd), and the symbol $\propto$ means "proportional to".

- **The gist, 5 minutes.** The [series page](index.qmd): one puzzle, its answer, and the idea behind the whole series.
- **The core idea.** Read [0 · What makes a sound a note?](note.qmd), [4 · Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?](violin.qmd) and [8 · Why does a drum thud?](drum.qmd), skipping the folds (about an hour); add [3 · Why does a loop of string land exactly on the lines?](circle.qmd) for the recipe in its simplest form. They carry the main idea: a pitch is a repeating sound, the string is a real instrument whose frequencies are whole-number multiples, and the drum is one whose frequencies are not. Page 3 shows, in the simplest case, where the lines on the ruler come from.
- **Every puzzle and its answer, about half an hour.** Each page's puzzle, demo and summary box, pages 0 to 10.
- **The whole story with the mathematics, about three and a half hours.** Pages 0 to 8 in order, each deriving its operator and its spectrum, and each answering the question the last one raised.
- **Everything, about four and a half hours.** All the pages, including [9 · Can you hear the shape of a drum?](shape.qmd) and the [epilogue](epilogue.qmd), with the folds open.

Here for one puzzle? The series page lists every page by its question, and each page says at the top which earlier page it builds on. Already know Fourier series? Start at page 4. The times assume reading about 120 words a minute, plus a minute or two per demo.

## All pages

In the table, $\partial_x$ means a derivative in $x$, so $-c^2\partial_x^2$ is the string's $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2$; $\kappa^2 = EI/\rho S$ is a bar's stiffness constant ([page 6](kalimba.qmd)); $\Delta$ is the [Laplacian](glossary.qmd#laplacian); [circulant](glossary.qmd#circulant) matrices and [Bessel](glossary.qmd#bessel) zeros are explained on pages 2 and 8.

| Page | New idea | Operator | Frequencies |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| [0 · What makes a sound a note?](note.qmd) | a note is a sound that repeats; its partials are whole-number multiples | | $f, 2f, 3f, \dots$ |
| [1 · Why does a fading note stay in tune?](oscillator.qmd) | one restoring force, one frequency | the number $k/m$ | $\sqrt{k/m}/2\pi$ |
| [2 · How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?](ring.qmd) | many masses: eigenvectors of a matrix | circulant matrix | $\propto \sin(\pi k/N)$ |
| [3 · Why does a loop of string land exactly on the lines?](circle.qmd) | the smallest operator spectrum; Fourier series | $-c^2\,d^2/d\theta^2$ on a loop | $\propto n$, exactly |
| [★ The spectrum of an operator](spectrum.qmd) | the recipe: Newton's law → operator → spectrum → sound, on every instrument | $u_{tt} = -Au$ | $\sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi$ |
| [4 · Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?](violin.qmd) | boundary conditions are part of the operator | $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2$, ends tied | $\propto n$ |
| [5 · Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?](clarinet.qmd) | closing one end halves the lowest frequency and keeps only its odd multiples | the same, on pressure | $\propto 2n - 1$ |
| [6 · Why does a kalimba sound clean?](kalimba.qmd) | bending: four derivatives spread the overtones; the clamped and free ends move them off the whole numbers | $\kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$ | $1 : 6.27 : 17.55$ |
| [6b · Where did the harmonica reed's overtones go?](harmonica.qmd) | the excitation, not the operator, can set the overtones | the same as 6 | heard as $\propto n$ |
| [7 · Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?](piano.qmd) | operators add; the pedals act on damping and forcing, not on the spectrum | $-c^2\partial_x^2 + \kappa^2\partial_x^4$ | $n\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}$ |
| [8 · Why does a drum thud?](drum.qmd) | two dimensions; no clear pitch | $-c^2\Delta$ on a disk | Bessel zeros |
| [9 · Can you hear the shape of a drum?](shape.qmd) | the spectrum hears area and perimeter, but not always the shape | $-c^2\Delta$ on any region | Weyl's law |
| [10 · Did instruments shape our scales?](epilogue.qmd) | the spectrum decides which intervals sound smooth | the bar's, with free ends | $1 : 2.76 : 5.40$ |

: Every page, its new idea, its operator and its frequencies. {.striped}

## Families

<details><summary>Instruments that are the same up to constants</summary>

Instruments in one family share one rule for the restoring force, so they are close to the same mathematical object with different constants. The last column says what still differs inside a family: for air columns the ends, which are part of the operator, and for drums the air around the head, which matters for timpani.

| Family | Operator and boundary | Demos | What varies inside the family |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Strings under tension | $-c^2\partial_x^2$, tied ends | [Violin](violin.qmd) | length, tension, mass per length; plucked (guitar, harp) or bowed (violin, cello) |
| Air columns | $-c^2\partial_x^2$ on pressure | [Clarinet](clarinet.qmd), with a flute switch | the boundary condition: one end closed (clarinet, pan pipes) or both open (flute) |
| Clamped bars | $\kappa^2\partial_x^4$, clamped base, free tip | [Kalimba](kalimba.qmd), [Harmonica](harmonica.qmd) | steel tine or brass reed; plucked or blown, which decides whether you hear harmonics |
| Stiff strings | $-c^2\partial_x^2 + \kappa^2\partial_x^4$, pinned ends | [Piano](piano.qmd) | stiffness, rising toward the treble |
| Membranes | $-c^2\Delta$ on a disk | [Drum](drum.qmd) | tension and size; the air under a timpani head |

</details>


## Comparison

**Every instrument side by side**: force, operator, boundary, eigen-condition, ratios, excitation.

| | Violin | Clarinet | Kalimba | Harmonica | Piano | Drum |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Restoring force | tension | air pressure | bending | bending | tension + bending | tension, in 2D |
| Newton's law on | a segment | a slab of air | a slice: torque, then force | a slice, as for the kalimba | a segment, both forces added | a patch, via the divergence theorem |
| Operator | $-c^2\partial_x^2$ | $-c^2\partial_x^2$ on pressure | $\kappa^2\partial_x^4$ | $\kappa^2\partial_x^4$ | $-c^2\partial_x^2+\kappa^2\partial_x^4$ | $-c^2\Delta$ |
| Boundary | $u=0$ at both ends | $p_x=0$ at reed, $p=0$ at open end | $u=u'=0$ at clamp, $u''=u'''=0$ at tip | same as the kalimba | $u=u''=0$ at both ends | $u=0$ on the rim |
| Eigen-condition | $\sin kL=0$ | $\cos kL=0$ | $\cos\beta L\cosh\beta L=-1$ | $\cos\beta L\cosh\beta L=-1$ | $\sin kL=0$ | $J_m(ka)=0$ |
| Mode ratios | $n$ | $2n-1$ | 1, 6.27, 17.55 | 1, 6.27, 17.55 | $n\sqrt{(1+Bn^2)/(1+B)}$ | 1, 1.59, 2.14 |
| Excitation | bow, sustained | reed, sustained | thumb pluck | airflow, sustained | felt hammer | stick |
| What you hear | exact harmonics | odd harmonics dominate; overblows a [twelfth](glossary.qmd#octave) | pitch plus a brief clink | exact harmonics, from the chopped airflow | near-harmonic; stretched octaves | inharmonic: a thud |



```{=html}
<script src="core.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core, M = C.models;
  var DEF = {
    violin: function () { return M.violin.partials(); },
    clarinet: function () { return M.clarinet.partials(); },
    kalimba: function () { return M.kalimba.partials(); },
    harmonica: function () { return M.harmonica.partials(); },
    piano: function () { return M.piano.partials({ B: 0.0012 }); },
    drum: function () { return M.drum.partials({ r: 0.35 }); }
  };
  var SUSTAINED = { violin: 1, clarinet: 1, harmonica: 1 };
  function draw() {
    document.querySelectorAll("svg[data-mini]").forEach(function (svg) {
      C.stems(svg, DEF[svg.getAttribute("data-mini")](), { W: 200, H: 58, rmax: 8, fs: 9, sw: 2, labelEvery: 2, noOff: true });
    });
    document.querySelectorAll("[data-ratios]").forEach(function (el) {
      el.textContent = DEF[el.getAttribute("data-ratios")]().map(function (p) { return p.ratio; }).sort(function (a, b) { return a - b; }).slice(0, 4).map(function (r) { return r.toFixed(2); }).join(", ");
    });
  }
  function fadeOut(buf, sec) { var d = buf.getChannelData(0), n = Math.floor(sec * buf.sampleRate); for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) d[d.length - 1 - i] *= i / n; return buf; }
  document.querySelectorAll("[data-play]").forEach(function (b) {
    b.addEventListener("click", function () {
      var id = b.getAttribute("data-play"), f = M[id].F0, buf;
      if (SUSTAINED[id]) buf = fadeOut(C.render(C.toHz(DEF[id](), f), 1.8), 0.4);
      else buf = C.render(C.toHz(DEF[id](), f), id === "piano" ? 3.2 : 2.6);
      C.play(buf, 0.8);
    });
  });
  C.onTheme(draw);
  draw();
})();
</script>
```
